question: What's your criterion? How do you decide what Jesus actually said?
subtitle: Also the Marcion charge
aliases: which parts of the Bible do you trust
finding: We have a stated method, it is public, and it is applied the same way to passages we like and passages we don't. Four tools: multiple independent attestation; the direction of redaction (we distrust an editorial change that moves toward the editor's known theology and away from his own written source); the criterion of embarrassment (we trust material preserved against the preserver's interest); and the manuscript record itself, which is physical evidence. We are not claiming the Bible is corrupt. We are claiming it has an editorial history that textual critics of every persuasion already document, visible at specific, nameable seams. The method is not a modern invention: in the Clementine literature an ancient opponent asks Peter the exact question we get asked, and gets a criterion in reply.
oneLiners: Everyone reads with a criterion. Ours is written down. Ask him for his.
We're not saying the Bible is corrupted. We're saying it was edited, in specific places, and the manuscripts are where we found out.
Matthew copied Mark and added five words. That's not a theory; you can lay the two columns side by side.
Marcion kept Paul and burned the Hebrew Bible. We keep the Hebrew Bible and question Paul. We're his photographic negative.
A method that can't lose isn't a method. Ours loses Mark 10:45 and we keep the verse anyway.
Our textual evidence comes from believing Christian scholars. You can't call it biased against you.
doNotSay: "The Bible is corrupted." A global claim we don't make. "Edited here, visibly, and here's the witness list" is a local claim, and the only kind we make.

Don't claim Jeremiah 8:8 proves the sacrificial legislation was falsified. The verse establishes that a canonical prophet accused the scribes of falsifying the written law; that it was the cult law is our inference from 7:21-22. Say "inference."
Don't exempt our own favorites. Matthew 25 passes on embarrassment, Matthew 11:30 is corroboration not a pillar, and Mark 10:45 we concede and argue the meaning.

When asked what would change your mind, answer it. A pre-Matthean source with the atonement clause; a second-century Greek witness to the Comma; Mark 16:9-20 in a fourth-century codex. Then ask it back.

sources.tier: red text · Case A, we prefer Mark
sources.note: Mark's cup saying. Matthew 26:28 copies it and adds "for the remission of sins": the clause is new, moves toward Matthew's fulfillment theology, and no other early witness has it. Flag it.
Not a manuscript variant but a redaction visible by direct comparison of a copy with its source.

sources.tier: red text · Case B, we prefer Matthew
sources.phrase: when saw we thee an hungred
sources.note: Single-source, and load-bearing for us. Does the criterion let us keep it? Yes: it hands salvation to people who didn't know who they were serving, gives nothing to Matthew's program, and takes the verdict out of the hands of the credentialed. Material that embarrasses its preserver is the strongest there is. Same tool, opposite outcomes, for reasons available to inspection.
In Q (Luke 16:17 too), affirming the permanence of Torah in the strongest terms. A Marcion-style reading would want it gone. We keep it and build the Torah card on it.
Earliest source, no redaction escape hatch. We concede the text and argue the meaning. If our method were "delete what's inconvenient," these two verses would be the first to go.

sources.tier: red text · embarrassment, against high Christology
sources.note: Jesus baptized by John for repentance; "none good but one" (10:18); Gethsemane; "why hast thou forsaken me" (15:34); "neither the Son" (13:32). The criterion of embarrassment is why we trust these. It cuts our way too: the Last Supper tradition is awkward for an anti-blood teacher and early and multiply attested. We don't deny the scene; we dispute one clause in one gospel.

sources.title: Homilies 2.38, the false pericopes
sources.edition: Thomas Smith, ANF vol. 8 (1886), public domain
sources.note: "The written law had added to it certain falsehoods contrary to the law of God." The doctrine is worked out across 3.42-51; the exchange is the striking part.

sources.title: Homilies 3.48-51, Simon asks for the criterion
sources.note: Simon: how do you recognize what in the law is true, mixed up with these falsehoods? Peter answers with a criterion, not a preference: the true Prophet's teaching is the test, applied with discernment, "be ye prudent money-changers," and "the things which He destroyed did not belong to the law" (3.51). A second-century Jewish-Christian text answering "what's your criterion?" with a criterion.

sources.phrase: the pen of the scribes is in vain
sources.note: A canonical prophet accusing the scribal class of falsifying the written law. The Hebrew is debated; that the falsification was the sacrificial legislation is our inference from 7:21-22. Say so.

"You've built a Bible out of your preferences." Everyone has a canon within a canon; the question is whether it's stated. Ask how they reconcile Leviticus 11 with Mark 7, Jeremiah 7:22 with Numbers 28, John 3:13 with Elijah's chariot. They'll call theirs "the clear teaching of scripture." Ours is written down with both test cases shown.

sources.title: Marcion, via Tertullian, Against Marcion
sources.edition: ANF vol. 3, public domain; not yet held
sources.note: "You've reinvented Marcion." The twenty-second answer: Marcion threw out the Hebrew Bible, the Hebrew God and the Jewish Jesus, and kept Paul. We keep the prophets, the Hebrew God and the Jewish Jesus, and question Paul. He wrote a new canon; we add nothing and remove nothing. The second-century group that held our position were the Ebionites, and Marcion's opponents and ours are the same people.

"This is the Jesus Seminar with extra steps." Jefferson took scissors to what a deist found reasonable. We keep the apocalyptic sayings, the exorcisms, the judgment language, the Torah affirmations and Mark 10:45, all awkward for a tidy modern reading. Source-critical, not taste-critical: ours keeps more of the strange material, not less.

sources.phrase: the new testament in my blood
sources.note: "Any text you dislike becomes redaction." Then falsify it. The method predicts: if Matthew's clause is redactional it should be missing from Mark, Luke, Paul and the Didache, and it is. If Mark's longer ending were original it should be in our oldest codices, and it isn't. Show a passage where we claim redaction and the manuscripts go against us, and we'll drop the claim.

"The scholars who catalogued those variants still believe in substitutionary atonement." Correct, and it's one of the strongest things about our evidence. Metzger was a devout Presbyterian; the brackets around Mark 16:9-20 were put there by committees of believing Christians. We disagree with them about theology, on top of shared evidence. "Yes, which is why you can't call them biased against you."

sources.tier: the seams · KJV prints it, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus don't
sources.note: The longer ending, 16:9-20: absent from our two oldest complete codices, multiple competing endings survive, bracketed in nearly every modern Bible.

sources.tier: the seams · KJV prints it, no Greek manuscript before the 14th century
sources.note: The Comma Johanneum: no Greek manuscript before the 14th century, no Greek father cites it, a Latin marginal gloss that migrated into the text.

sources.tier: the seams · absent from the earliest witnesses, and it floats
sources.note: The pericope adulterae (7:53-8:11): absent from the earliest witnesses; some manuscripts place it in Luke. None of this is our claim; it is in the apparatus of every critical edition and the footnotes of the Bible in the other person's hand.
